Find Your Drive Size

Start with your application (optional): tap a Design Intent below to pre-filter the drive-type pool using the Drive/Socket Profile ratings, before you even touch thread size or standard.

Understanding the attributes The rating features describe what a drive type is naturally good at, no matter which size you choose. Torque Capacity and Cam-Out Resistance show how much twisting force it can handle before the tool slips out. Automation Fit shows whether it works well with a power screwdriver or assembly robot, or really needs a careful hand. Tamper Resistance shows how hard it is for someone without the right tool to remove. Since these describe the drive TYPE itself (Internal Hex, Torx, Phillips, and so on) rather than a specific size, you can compare them across every row on this page.

Drive Size Selection Best Practices

1. Verify Against Engineering Drawings

Always confirm drive size specifications match the controlling engineering drawing. Manufacturing drawings take precedence over estimates or tool references. Check for any design-specific requirements such as custom tool sizes or drive type restrictions.

2. Account for Manufacturing Variations

Drive size can vary significantly by fastener manufacturer, recess depth, head diameter, strength class, and surface coating. Identical fastener part numbers from different suppliers may require different hex key or socket sizes. Always source test samples before committing to production assembly procedures.

3. Standardize Tool Inventory

Before finalizing fastener selections, review your available tooling inventory. Standardizing on drive types and sizes that match existing tools reduces assembly errors, improves field serviceability, and minimizes training requirements. If a line uses powered or robotic screwdriving, check the Automation Fit rating in this tool's Drive/Socket Profile before locking in a drive type -- it flags which drives engage reliably without an operator holding alignment by hand. Communicate standardization decisions with suppliers and manufacturing teams.

4. Consider Environmental Factors

Account for operating conditions that may affect drive integrity. Corrosive environments may require coatings that alter recess dimensions. High-vibration or high-torque applications call for a drive with strong Torque Capacity and Cam-Out Resistance ratings, shown in the Drive/Socket Profile for each result -- a drive that's easy to strip or slip out under load is a poor fit for those joints regardless of size. Cold-weather assembly may impact tooling clearances.

5. Plan for Field Service and Inspection

Select fastener drives based on tools available to service technicians and field inspectors. Specialty drive types may not be available in remote locations. Design for ease of inspection and maintenance using widely available tooling whenever possible.

6. Cross-Reference Multiple Standards

Use this tool to compare drive size recommendations across different standards (ISO, DIN, ASME, SAE). Standards differences may apply in global supply chains or multi-source procurement scenarios. Document which standard was applied in your final design.

7. Let the Drive/Socket Profile Guide Your Shortlist

Before narrowing down to a specific size, use the four Drive/Socket Profile ratings on this tool to shortlist which drive types even belong in the running for your application. Need to hold up under heavy torque or vibration? Look for strong Torque Capacity and Cam-Out Resistance -- Internal Hex, External Hex, Torx-style, and Square drives tend to lead here. Building on an automated or robotic line? Filter toward drives rated "Robotic-Ready" for Automation Fit so bits engage consistently without manual alignment. Designing an enclosure or fixture the end user shouldn't be able to open? Look for "Elevated" or "High" Tamper Resistance rather than defaulting to whatever drive is already on hand. Add a few candidates to the Comparison Table and sort by whichever rating matters most for the job to see the tradeoffs side by side.

Remember: This tool provides reference guidance based on industry standards. Drive size is one of many fastener selection criteria. Work with qualified engineers and suppliers to ensure fastener selections meet all performance, reliability, and compliance requirements for your specific application.

Disclaimer: This tool provides guidance based on common industry standards and practices.
